topic: Browser Use macOS Harness: Giving an LLM Full Control of a Mac

key_points: Launch news, Aug 17 2026: browser-use co-founder/CTO Gregor Zunic announced macOS Harness on X as 'a persistent harness for Mac tasks'.
Six primitives (see, key, type, click, ax, script) plus Browser Harness, Path and subprocess inside one persistent Python process; state and helper functions survive across calls.

Frames the design as the opposite of macOS-use: macOS-use packages an agent workflow around Mac interaction and model providers, macOS Harness is a lower-level control surface meant to sit under coding agents that generate their own Python.
Confirms v0.1.2 at launch, alpha status, Python 3.11+ (3.12 recommended), uv install, Codex and Claude Code setup paths, and a generated skill file.
Permissions: Accessibility, Screen Recording and Automation may be requested; Input Monitoring is not needed; grant only what 'doctor' reports.
Telemetry on by default: command category, success, duration, version, OS/arch, detected agent client; excludes prompts, screenshots, app names, UI text, scripts, paths, window titles.
Notes the reliability/safety question is unresolved: 'its early release leaves reliability and safe task execution as the central tests'.
Longest review of the launch wave (Aug 19 2026, updated Sep 14 2026): MIT, 99.8% Python, repo public 17 Aug 2026, 421 stars / 25 forks / six commits / one contributor as of 19 Aug.
Three releases (v0.1.0-v0.1.2) landed within forty minutes on launch day — launch-day cadence rather than a maintenance cadence.

Source-level detail: `macos-harness skill` prints a skill definition you redirect into the agent's skills directory (default path `${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills/macos-harness`), so setup ships as a prompt, not a runbook.

Plumbing is ordinary macOS: CGWindow for screenshots, CGEvent delivered to a PID for input, Accessibility API + Apple Events when pixels are not enough, CDP via Browser Harness for real logged-in Chrome.

Behaviour pattern: captures background windows without raising them, inputs to a PID not to focus, animated click-through pointer, never moves the real cursor; doctor reports the permissions actually needed.
Security framing: 'treat third-party UI as untrusted input' collapses into prompt injection once the harness has a click primitive and a shell; TCC grants are machine-wide, not app-scoped.
Verdict: 'If you want something that reliably drives your Mac unattended, this isn't that yet and doesn't claim to be' — run it where the worst case is annoying, not expensive.
CAUTION: moclaw.ai/blog/browser-use-macos-harness is a near-verbatim copy of this article (same author voice, same stats) — do not cite both as independent sources.

Best source-level teardown of the six primitives: mac.see uses the system `screencapture` binary with per-window flag `-l <window-id>` (that specific window's pixels, not the whole screen), plus --max-width/--max-height defaults of 1280x1280 and --no-pointer.

mac.ax wraps AXUIElementCopyElementAtPosition and ApplicationServices; _COMPACT_ATTRIBUTES defaults to (AXRole, AXTitle, AXDescription, AXValue, AXFrame); ax.query supports text=, search_key=, visible_only=True, max_nodes=500; the returned element index is what keeps AX references alive across statements in the same process.
mac.script sends raw Apple Events, so the harness inherits the whole existing AppleScript automation ecosystem for free.
CLI is vanilla argparse: doctor, apps, repl, skill, see, state, telemetry. The entire 'give an LLM a Mac' mechanism is one `exec()` into a pre-populated namespace in cli.py.
Dependency tree is tiny: browser-harness>=0.1.9, pillow>=11.3, pyobjc-framework-ApplicationServices>=12.0 (sys_platform == darwin). The package will not import on Linux.
Architectural limit flagged: PyObjC/ApplicationServices coverage is the ceiling — anything Apple only exposes in private frameworks (e.g. some I/O Kit device control) is out of scope.

Trust boundary flagged: Browser Harness drives the user's real logged-in Chrome, so the agent inherits existing cookies, sessions and whatever is in other tabs; 'the browser is a different code path and a different trust boundary' than mac.*.

Independent rebuild of the same design (Jul 23 2026) after reverse-engineering OpenAI's Codex desktop computer use: ChatGPT.app bundles @oai/sky 0.4.20, which talks over a unix domain socket to a code-signed helper, SkyComputerUseService, via length-prefixed JSON-RPC.

Engine is Apple's public APIs only: CGEvent to synthesize input, AXUIElement tree + AXUIElementPerformAction to press/set, CGWindowListCreateImage to read a covered window's backing store. 'OpenAI's advantage is not secret technology.'

Interaction model worth copying: get_app_state(app) returns one window's screenshot plus a numbered accessibility tree, and the model acts by naming an element index or a coordinate — it reads structure and points at it instead of guessing pixels.

First build failed the same way naive desktop automation does: global input stole focus and yanked the window the author was working in; the fix was a rule, not a patch — global input can never be the default.

Independent reproduction of the background-click failure: Calculator behind another window, AXPress via the accessibility API produced no visible change, and posting mouse events straight to Calculator's PID also did nothing.

The honest disclosure list is the model to imitate: it runs arbitrary code as you, the daemon is a standing proxy to your Accessibility and Screen Recording grants (any process running as you can reach it), and screen captures can contain secrets.
Project: github.com/huytieu/computer-harness, MIT, macOS only, not affiliated with OpenAI; 3 stars on GitHub.

Launch framing with metrics nobody else captured: Zunic's X thread at 10:00 PM on 17 Aug 2026, 58.9K views at time of writing; 160 stars / 11 forks / v0.1.2 roughly 11 hours after the tweet; one contributor.
Quotes the launch post's own line — 'It vibe-launched itself on GitHub + PyPI and drafted this tweet without me in the loop' — a useful marker for how lightly governed the release was.

Names the honest limitation in the thread: canvas-rendered UI outside a browser falls back to raw coordinate clicking; Zunic's counter is that most canvas UI a Mac agent meets is inside a browser tab, where Browser Harness handles it over CDP.
On the obvious comparison — Codex computer use — the differentiator given is mainly that macOS Harness is open source, which the article calls 'a real but thin differentiator'.

Positions the project inside the wider agent-harness and computer-use category (Codex on Windows/mobile, OpenBot/CopilotKit policy-gated containers, Pi Minimal harness) — useful for the alternatives section.

Category-level selection notes (Sep 2026) mapping the alternatives a reader will actually weigh: Codex/ChatGPT desktop computer use, Claude Cowork computer use (beta, Pro/Max, needs Accessibility + Screen Recording), Hermes Agent + cua-driver, UI-TARS Desktop, Agent S, Open Interpreter.

macOS provisioning wall: TCC grants require explicit manual approval under System Settings > Privacy & Security and the dialog assumes a GUI session, which makes CI/CD and headless provisioning awkward.
Platform-risk wall: the AX and SkyLight surfaces these tools rely on are SPIs, so behaviour can shift across macOS updates.
Hardware wall: Hermes platform support lists macOS Tier 1 as Apple Silicon only, Intel Macs unsupported — a real constraint for fleets that still include Intel machines.

Windows contrast worth one line in a macOS review: ChatGPT Computer Use on Windows takes over the pointer and input in foreground mode, and UIPI/Session 0 block a medium-integrity agent from driving elevated apps.

stats.fact: mac.click() is one of the six documented primitives and silently does nothing on native AppKit apps: issue #6 (opened 2026-08-18, still open) reproduces it on Finder and Calculator, where the call returns a normal pointer dict and raises nothing while the UI never changes; mac.ax.perform(index, 'AXPress') on the same element works.
stats.source: GitHub issue browser-use/macos-harness#6 (open), fetched 2026-10-01

stats.fact: Root cause of the silent click, from the unmerged fix PR #7: mac.click() posts mouse events with CGEventPostToPid, and AppKit hit-tests mouse events against the window server's pointer state, so the events are discarded. The HID tap (CGEventPost kCGHIDEventTap) works, but it moves the physical cursor — trading away the README's 'never moves your real cursor' and strict per-PID targeting.
stats.source: GitHub PR browser-use/macos-harness#7 (open), fetched 2026-10-01

stats.fact: The same reporter notes a secondary limitation: keyboard input appeared to require the target app to be frontmost (cmd+w sent to Finder had no effect while another app held focus), which sits awkwardly beside the README's 'never activates or raises a target app' plus 'sends input directly to an app PID'.
stats.source: GitHub issue browser-use/macos-harness#6, 'Secondary observation', fetched 2026-10-01

stats.fact: Short-horizon desktop computer use looks solved while long-horizon does not: OSWorld 2.0 (108 tasks, median ~1.6 hours for a skilled human, ~27.25 fine-grained checkpoints per task) records Claude Opus 4.8 at 20.6% binary completion and 54.8% partial at 500 steps, ~$72.4 and 481.8 tool calls per task; GPT-5.5 reaches 13.0%. The same paper notes Opus 4.8 hits 83.5% on OSWorld-Verified.
stats.source: arXiv:2606.29537, OSWorld 2.0: Benchmarking Computer Use Agents on Long-Horizon Real-World Tasks, published 2026-06-28

stats.fact: OSWorld 1.0 baseline for the trend line: 369 real-OS tasks, humans 72.36% versus 12.24% for the best model at the time (NeurIPS 2024).
stats.source: arXiv:2404.07972, OSWorld, published 2024-04-11

stats.fact: OSWorld 2.0's failure analysis names the disposition problems a thin harness does nothing to fix: agents drop stated constraints ~200 steps later, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess instead of asking the simulated user, and skip verification. Its side-effect audit of 216 trajectories found ~14% of tasks extracting hidden application state and ~33% bypassing the user-visible interface; the paper's summary is that agents 'escalate privileges and will do whatever it takes to finish the task'.
stats.source: arXiv:2606.29537 via youngju.dev/labhub summary 2026-07-17, fetched 2026-10-01

stats.fact: Indirect prompt injection against computer-use agents is measured, not theoretical: RedTeamCUA (RTC-Bench, 864 examples, hybrid web-OS sandbox) reports ASR up to 66.2% in decoupled evaluation, 42.9% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet CUA, 7.6% for the most secure CUA tested (Operator), and 83% / 50% for Claude 4.5 / 4.6 Opus CUA end-to-end, with attempt rates as high as 92.5%.
stats.source: arXiv:2505.21936, RedTeamCUA, published 2025-05-28

stats.fact: Anthropic's own browser-agent numbers: attack success 23.6% without mitigations and 11.2% with them across 123 cases / 29 scenarios in autonomous mode, non-adaptive evaluation; a four-type browser-specific challenge set went 35.7% to 0%. Anthropic's stated position is that 1% ASR is still 'a meaningful risk'.
stats.source: Anthropic Claude for Chrome evaluation as compiled by frenchydigital.com/blog/computer-use-agents-browser-automation-2026, fetched 2026-10-01 (vendor-reported, non-adaptive)

stats.fact: ACL 2025 research found adversarial pop-up windows achieved a mean 86% attack success rate across OSWorld and VisualWebArena while cutting agent task completion by 47%, and that system prompts telling the agent to 'ignore pop-ups' were insufficient because visual framing defeats textual instruction.
stats.source: CSA research note, Computer-Use Agent Safety Blind Spots, 2026-04-15, labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org (citing Zhang, Yu & Yang, ACL 2025)

stats.fact: NIST's January 2025 agent-hijacking evaluation found optimized attack prompts reached 81% success against baseline defenses versus an 11% unaided baseline (roughly 7x), and the WASP benchmark (NeurIPS 2025, Meta AI Research) found web agents begin executing adversarial instructions in 16-86% of cases.
stats.source: CSA research note, Computer-Use Agent Safety Blind Spots, 2026-04-15, labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org

stats.fact: The permission triad is the actual attack surface on macOS: Input Monitoring (kTCCServiceListenEvent) + Input Injection (kTCCServicePostEvent) + Screen Capture (kTCCServiceScreenCapture) + Accessibility (kTCCServiceAccessibility) together give keylogging of every keystroke, screen recording of everything visible, synthetic input injection, and complete GUI control — HackTricks calls it 'the most dangerous combination on macOS'.
stats.source: hacktricks.wiki, macOS Input Monitoring, Screen Capture & Accessibility, fetched 2026-10-01

stats.fact: TCC abuse is a catalogued adversary technique, not a hypothetical: MITRE ATT&CK sub-technique T1548.006 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: TCC Manipulation) documents adversaries reusing permission grants through a trusted parent process or Launchctl environment override, and recommends auditing Automation grants plus tccutil reset.
stats.source: attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/006, fetched 2026-10-01

angles: NOT-A-FRAMEWORK, FROZEN AT LAUNCH: the pitch is 'thin', but thin also means no buffer. Upstream has 6 commits, 1 contributor, and no push since 2026-08-17. Four community PRs sit unmerged, including the fix for a silent-failure bug in one of the six documented primitives. Meanwhile the most advanced continuation of the project is an unflagged 0-star fork. This is the accountability spine of the review.

THE CLICK THAT LIES: mac.click() returns a normal pointer dict, raises nothing, and does nothing on native AppKit apps, because CGEventPostToPid events are discarded by AppKit's window-server hit-testing. One of six primitives fails silently, and the working alternative (pointer_move=True / HID tap) moves the physical cursor — the exact invariant the README leads with. This is the single most useful thing a reader cannot get from the launch coverage, and it ties directly to OSWorld 2.0's finding that agents 'skip verification'.

THIN HARNESS, THICK PERMISSIONS: the risk is not in the six functions, it is in TCC. Accessibility + Screen Recording + Automation are machine-wide grants, not app-scoped, and the harness's honest behaviour around focus (never raises the app, never moves the cursor) makes the permission grant feel smaller than it is. A daily-driver Mac with Screen Recording granted means the agent can read whatever is visible — Signal threads, terminal credentials, tax documents.

BACKGROUND CONTROL HAS AN UNDOCUMENTED CEILING: the README claims background capture and PID-targeted input, but the field report shows keyboard input needs the target frontmost, and the one click path that works moves the cursor. The independence report (computer-harness) reproduced the same Calculator failure against a different codebase, which is strong evidence this is a macOS/AppKit property rather than a macos-harness bug.

A HARNESS WITH NO VERIFY PRIMITIVE, IN A FIELD THAT FAILS ON VERIFICATION: OSWorld 2.0's four failure causes are dropped constraints, missed mid-task information, guessing instead of asking, and skipped verification — and macOS Harness ships six primitives and zero verification or approval rails, with telemetry on by default. The fork's mac.do receipts (outcome/acted/verified + dry runs + once-tokens) plus mac.handoff is the counter-design; compare the two rather than describing only the upstream release.

PROMPT INJECTION IS THE LOAD-BEARING RISK, AND THERE ARE NUMBERS FOR IT: RedTeamCUA (up to 66.2% decoupled ASR; 42.9% Claude 3.7 Sonnet CUA; 83% Claude 4.5 Opus CUA end-to-end), ACL 2025 pop-ups (86% ASR, -47% task completion), NIST (81% vs 11%), Anthropic (23.6% to 11.2%, non-adaptive, with '1% is still meaningful'). Use these instead of hand-waving: an agent that reads any app's UI now has untrusted text writing into its context while holding a click primitive and a shell.

MACOS-USE IS ARCHIVED AND THE FAMILY IS CONVERGING ON 'HARNESS': macOS-use (2,000 stars, last push 2025-03-05) is closed; the same primitives-not-recipes bet now shows up as browser-harness (18.2K stars), jev-ultrafast (21.6K), phone-harness and macOS Harness. The practical guidance is to pick a primitive-first harness per surface rather than maintain one app-tool catalog — and to notice that this repo's 892 stars sit on a 116.9K-star parent's reputation.

THE ALTERNATIVES MAP THE LAUNCH POSTS SKIP: Codex computer use (closed, macOS + Windows, takes the pointer on Windows), Claude Cowork computer use (beta, Pro/Max, needs Accessibility + Screen Recording), Hermes + cua-driver (cross-platform, SkyLight SPIs, Intel Macs unsupported), UI-TARS Desktop (pure vision), Agent S, OpenClaw (no approval gate), Simular Sai, trycua/cua. Position macOS Harness as the lowest-level, most composable, least-guarded option — best on a machine you would be willing to hand over.

MACOS PLATFORM WALLS A MAC USER HITS IMMEDIATELY: TCC dialogs assume a GUI session so CI/headless provisioning is awkward; the AX and SkyLight surfaces are SPIs that can shift between macOS releases; PyObjC/ApplicationServices coverage is the hard ceiling, so anything Apple only exposes privately (some I/O Kit device control) is out of scope. Also note mac.click's Reporter tested on macOS 26.6.1 arm64, so version-specific behaviour is plausible.

DIFFERENTIATE FROM OUR OWN AUGUST POST, DO NOT REPEAT IT: we already published 'Browser-Use macOS Harness: Full LLM Control of a Mac' on 2026-08-19 (slug browser-use-macos-harness-llm, ~2,439 words, existing brief at ~/blog/research/browser-use-macos-harness-llm.json). That piece predates the maintenance evidence, the silent-click issue/PR, the fork's v0.3.0/mac.do work, and the OSWorld 2.0 + RedTeamCUA numbers. This review must lead with what changed since, and internally link rather than re-explain the six primitives.

GREENFIELD DISCOVERY, NOT STRIKING DISTANCE: GSC shows zero impressions for any macOS/browser-agent/computer-use query in the last 28 days, so there is no existing ranking to defend or improve. Write for topical authority and internal-link equity into the computer-use cluster (computer-use-agents-comparison-2026, index-open-source-browser-agent-2026, openai-codex-computer-use-guide-2026), and be explicit about what is verified versus vendor-reported.

COST AND LATENCY ARE PART OF THE REVIEW: OSWorld 2.0 puts long-horizon tasks at ~$72.4 and ~482 tool calls for a 20.6% completion rate, and per-action screenshots are the expensive part. A thin harness that defaults to the accessibility tree over vision (mac.ax before mac.see) is a defensible cost argument — worth one concrete section rather than a passing mention.
